title: Benign and Premalignant Skin Lesions
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains the common growths of skin and oral mucosa and sorts them by what drives them and what they can become. Some are purely benign clonal proliferations (seborrheic keratosis, lipoma, cysts, cherry hemangioma), some are dysplastic lesions that sit on the path to carcinoma (actinic keratosis, oral leukoplakia), some mark systemic risk rather than local danger (dysplastic nevi), and a few announce an internal cancer through paraneoplastic mechanisms. Board questions describe a lesion by site, age, texture, and course, then ask for the mechanism, the histology, or the risk. The reasoning is the same each time: which cell is proliferating, what started it, and whether its nuclei are atypical.
prerequisites: Normal epidermal layers, keratinocyte maturation, and the granular layer (IN-1)
Melanocyte biology, the nevus growth sequence, and nest location (IN-13-A)
Cell cycle control through p53, Rb, p16, CDK4 and CDK6, and oncogene-induced senescence
Difference between hyperplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and invasive carcinoma
Granulomatous and foreign body inflammation, including giant cell formation

connections.how: Actinic keratosis and oral leukoplakia are the dysplastic stage of the same squamous pathway that ends in squamous cell carcinoma, and dysplastic nevi mark the host at risk for melanoma.
Leser-Trelat sign and malignant acanthosis nigricans point to gastric adenocarcinoma, so a skin finding becomes a reason to look at the stomach.
Most acanthosis nigricans is driven by hyperinsulinemia acting through IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes, which links the lesion to insulin resistance rather than cancer.
Oral hairy leukoplakia is EBV replication in tongue epithelium under immunosuppression, and thrush is Candida overgrowth, so both read as host defense failures.

Vascular birthmarks separate into true endothelial tumors and developmental malformations, and a somatic GNAQ mutation in one embryonic field explains the face, meninges, and eye findings of Sturge-Weber syndrome.

terms.def: Disordered growth with nuclear atypia and loss of normal maturation that involves part, but not the full thickness, of an epithelium.
Atypia through the entire epithelial thickness with the basement membrane still intact.
Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum because keratinocyte maturation is faulty, which gives the cornified layer a rough adherent scale.
Accumulation of degenerated, blue-gray elastic and collagen material in the upper dermis from chronic ultraviolet exposure.
A covalent link between adjacent pyrimidine bases formed when DNA absorbs UVB directly, repaired by nucleotide excision repair.
A permanent growth arrest triggered when a strong proliferative signal such as mutant BRAF drives expression of p16 and related cell cycle inhibitors, which is why most nevi stay small.
Disordered arrangement of melanocytic nests, including bridging between adjacent rete ridges and lentiginous single-cell growth along the basal layer.
A round intraepidermal collection of laminated keratin seen within a seborrheic keratosis, also called a pseudo-horn cyst when it is a surface invagination.
A finding caused by tumor-derived mediators or tumor-driven immunity rather than by local tumor growth or metastasis.
Velvety hyperpigmented papillomatous plaques of the neck, axillae, and flexures from keratinocyte and fibroblast growth signaling.
A developmental error in vessel formation that is present at birth, grows only with the child, and does not involute.
A white mucosal plaque that cannot be scraped off and has no other specific diagnosis, which may harbor dysplasia detectable only on histology.

sections.title: Actinic keratosis: ultraviolet injury, keratinocyte dysplasia, and progression

blocks.text: Actinic keratosis is a focus of dysplastic keratinocytes produced by cumulative ultraviolet exposure. It appears on chronically sun-exposed skin: the face, bald scalp, ears, lateral neck, forearms, and dorsal hands. Risk rises with age, fair skin (Fitzpatrick types I and II), outdoor work, and immunosuppression, and the lesions tend to be multiple because the whole field has been irradiated for decades.

UVB (about 280 to 320 nm) is absorbed directly by DNA and joins adjacent pyrimidines into cyclobutane dimers. Nucleotide excision repair removes most of them, but repair is imperfect. A cytosine held inside a dimer deaminates to uracil much faster than normal, and replication across the unrepaired lesion places adenine opposite it, so a cytosine and guanine pair becomes a thymine and adenine pair. This is why the ultraviolet signature mutation is a C to T transition at dipyrimidine sites. When this hits TP53, the keratinocyte loses the p53-dependent arrest and apoptosis that normally eliminate UV-damaged cells. The mutant clone survives further exposure, expands from the basal layer upward, and acquires additional changes in pathways such as NOTCH and CDKN2A. UVA contributes indirectly through reactive oxygen species. Chronic UV also suppresses local immune surveillance, which is why transplant recipients accumulate these lesions rapidly.

The clinical findings follow the biology. Because the atypical cells mature poorly, nuclei persist in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis) and the cornified layer becomes adherent and gritty, so the lesion is often easier to feel than to see: a rough, sandpaper-like, erythematous scaly papule or plaque a few millimeters across. Histology shows atypia confined to the lower epidermis with alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis, often sparing the follicular and sweat duct openings, together with solar elastosis in the dermis as evidence of the cumulative dose. A hypertrophic lesion may build a cutaneous horn.

Progression is a matter of degree, not of kind. Partial-thickness atypia is dysplasia; full-thickness atypia with an intact basement membrane is squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease); breach of the basement membrane is invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Any single actinic keratosis has a low annual probability of progressing, on the order of a fraction of one percent per lesion per year, but a patient with many lesions over many years carries a substantial cumulative risk. Induration, tenderness, rapid growth, bleeding, or a diameter over about 1 cm raises concern that invasion has already occurred.

blocks.predict: A transplant recipient on long-term immunosuppression develops dozens of actinic keratoses within three years, while an age-matched neighbor with the same sun history has four. What accounts for the difference?
blocks.explain: Both have similar mutational burden from accumulated UV, but immunosuppression removes the T cell surveillance that normally eliminates antigenic dysplastic clones, so more clones persist and expand.

sections.title: Dysplastic nevi: atypia, the senescence brake, and melanoma risk

blocks.text: A common acquired nevus starts when a melanocyte acquires an activating mutation in BRAF (most often V600E) or NRAS. The mutant cell proliferates in a burst, then the same strong MAP kinase signal drives expression of p16, the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor encoded by CDKN2A, and the clone enters oncogene-induced senescence. This brake is why an ordinary nevus is small, symmetric, uniform in color, and stable for decades.

Dysplastic nevi are melanocytic proliferations in which the brake holds only partly. They are usually larger than common nevi, commonly over 5 mm, with irregular or ill-defined borders, variable tan to dark brown pigment, and a flat peripheral rim around a slightly raised center. They occur on sun-exposed and covered skin, including the scalp, buttocks, and breasts, which tells you that UV is a contributor but not the whole story.

Biopsy shows two kinds of disorder. Cytologic atypia means enlarged, hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei in melanocytes that are larger than their neighbors. Architectural atypia means disordered placement: elongation of rete ridges with lentiginous single-cell growth along the basal layer, nests that fuse and bridge between adjacent rete ridges, and, in the dermal papillae, lamellar and concentric eosinophilic fibrosis with a patchy lymphocytic infiltrate and melanophages.

The risk message is epidemiologic, not local. Any individual dysplastic nevus very rarely becomes melanoma, and most melanomas arise in previously normal skin. What matters is the phenotype: having many dysplastic nevi identifies a person whose melanocytes carry a heavy mutational load and weakened senescence, so the raised risk is spread across all of the skin rather than concentrated in the atypical moles themselves. In familial atypical multiple mole melanoma, germline loss of CDKN2A removes p16, so CDK4 and CDK6 phosphorylate Rb without restraint and both the G1 checkpoint and the senescence response weaken. These families show many atypical nevi, melanoma at a younger age, multiple primaries, and in some kindreds pancreatic adenocarcinoma. A smaller number carry activating CDK4 mutations, which disable the same checkpoint from the other side.

blocks.caption: A nevus is normally self-limiting because its own driver mutation triggers the brake; losing p16 removes the brake and allows atypical growth.

blocks.title: Common nevus, dysplastic nevus, and melanoma

blocks.title: Worked example: why counting moles beats watching one mole
blocks.text: A 28-year-old woman has about 60 nevi, 12 of them larger than 5 mm with irregular borders, and a mother and maternal uncle who had melanoma before age 45. One atypical nevus is removed and reported as a dysplastic nevus with moderate atypia, fully excised. Does that excision address her risk? No. The removed lesion itself had a very small chance of becoming melanoma, and her danger comes from germline CDKN2A-type loss of the senescence checkpoint in every melanocyte she has. Her future melanoma is more likely to appear in skin that looks normal today, including the scalp and covered sites, because the weakened checkpoint is systemic while the excision was local.

sections.title: Seborrheic keratosis: a benign clonal epidermal proliferation

blocks.text: Seborrheic keratosis is the most common benign epidermal tumor of older adults. Lesions begin in middle age, increase in number with time, and favor the trunk, face, and neck, although they appear almost anywhere except palms, soles, and mucosa. They are sharply demarcated, tan to dark brown or black, waxy or verrucous plaques that look pasted or stuck onto the surface rather than growing into it. The surface often shows plugged follicular openings, which appear on dermoscopy as comedo-like openings and milia-like cysts.

The appearance follows directly from the architecture. These are clonal proliferations of small, uniform basaloid keratinocytes that grow upward and outward from the level of the surrounding basal layer, so the lesion sits above the skin line with a flat base and a sharp lateral edge. Acanthosis (thickened epidermis) and hyperkeratosis give the waxy bulk, invaginations of the surface and intraepidermal keratin collections form horn cysts and pseudo-horn cysts, and melanin within the basaloid cells accounts for the color. There is hyperpigmentation without melanocytic proliferation, so a dark seborrheic keratosis is still an epidermal, not a melanocytic, lesion. Recognized variants include the stucco keratosis of the lower legs, dermatosis papulosa nigra on the face in darkly pigmented skin, and the irritated or inflamed keratosis with squamous eddies after friction or trauma.

Many lesions carry activating mutations in FGFR3 or in PIK3CA, which drive keratinocyte proliferation through the MAP kinase and PI3 kinase pathways. The important point for the exam is that these are activating mutations in a growth pathway without the loss of checkpoint control seen in dysplasia: nuclei stay uniform, maturation remains orderly, there is no significant atypia, and the lesions do not become malignant.

Number and tempo carry the clinical signal. Slow accumulation over years is ordinary aging skin. The sudden eruption of many seborrheic keratoses over weeks to months, particularly with pruritus, is the Leser-Trelat sign and raises concern for an internal malignancy, classically gastric adenocarcinoma, with lymphoma and other adenocarcinomas also reported. The proposed mechanism is tumor-derived growth factor activity, such as transforming growth factor alpha acting on the epidermal growth factor receptor of keratinocytes, which is the same signaling logic behind malignant acanthosis nigricans and explains why the two signs often appear together. The association is debated because seborrheic keratoses are so common in the age group that also develops cancer, so the finding is a prompt to evaluate rather than proof of a tumor.

sections.title: Mucocutaneous paraneoplastic signs and their tumor associations

blocks.text: A paraneoplastic sign is produced by mediators the tumor releases or by immunity the tumor provokes, not by local invasion or metastasis. In the skin this happens through two mechanisms: tumor-derived growth factors that drive keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation, and tumor antigens that elicit antibodies or T cells which cross-react with normal skin and muscle. Both can appear before the cancer is found, which is why the skin finding sometimes directs the search.

In the growth factor group, eruptive seborrheic keratoses (Leser-Trelat sign) and malignant acanthosis nigricans share a proposed pathway: transforming growth factor alpha from the tumor, classically a gastric adenocarcinoma, stimulates the epidermal growth factor receptor on keratinocytes, which produces papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and epidermal thickening. Acanthosis nigricans gives velvety, hyperpigmented, thickened plaques in the axillae, posterior neck, and other flexures. The great majority of cases are not paraneoplastic at all: hyperinsulinemia from obesity, type 2 diabetes, or polycystic ovary syndrome spills over onto IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts and produces the identical lesion. The features that shift suspicion toward cancer are abrupt onset, a thin or weight-losing older adult, extensive or unusual sites including the palms and oral mucosa, and associated pruritus.

In the immune group, dermatomyositis in an adult carries a meaningful risk of underlying malignancy, especially ovarian, lung, gastric, colorectal, and pancreatic cancer and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; the risk is highest within the first few years of diagnosis and is lower in children. Its skin findings reflect interface injury and vasculopathy: a heliotrope violaceous periorbital rash, Gottron papules over the knuckles, a shawl or V-sign photodistributed erythema, and dilated nailfold capillaries, with proximal muscle weakness from perifascicular muscle injury. Paraneoplastic pemphigus occurs with lymphoid neoplasms, most often chronic lymphocytic leukemia and non-Hodgkin lymphoma and Castleman disease, and is driven by autoantibodies against desmogleins together with plakin proteins such as envoplakin and periplakin; the broader antigen target explains its severe, treatment-resistant oral erosions and its lichenoid as well as blistering features.

sections.title: Epidermal inclusion cyst, trichilemmal cyst, and lipoma

blocks.text: An epidermal inclusion cyst is a dermal cavity lined by stratified squamous epithelium that matures the way surface epidermis does, including a granular layer. It arises when surface or follicular infundibular epithelium is displaced into the dermis, by trauma or by plugging of the follicular opening, and then continues its normal program: it keratinizes through a granular layer and sheds soft, flaky, laminated keratin into the lumen. Clinically it is a mobile, dome-shaped dermal or subcutaneous nodule, often with a central punctum, that discharges cheesy, malodorous material. The common name sebaceous cyst is a misnomer because the contents are keratin, not sebum.

Keratin is inert while it stays inside an epithelial lining and strongly irritating once it escapes. Rupture, usually after squeezing or trauma, spills keratin into the dermis, where macrophages fuse into foreign body giant cells around the keratin flakes and a brisk neutrophilic and granulomatous reaction follows. The result is a red, hot, tender, swollen nodule that mimics an abscess but is usually sterile at first, which is why the exam stem describes an inflamed cyst with giant cells engulfing keratin rather than a bacterial infection. Multiple epidermal cysts in unusual numbers or sites, especially with osteomas and desmoid tumors, should raise the question of Gardner syndrome.

A trichilemmal or pilar cyst comes from the outer root sheath of the follicular isthmus, which keratinizes abruptly without forming a granular layer. Its lining shows cells that enlarge and then transition sharply to dense, compact, homogeneous keratin, and the contents are firm rather than flaky; calcification is common. About 90 percent occur on the scalp, they are frequently multiple, and familial cases with autosomal dominant inheritance are described. The single histologic discriminator worth memorizing is the granular layer: present in the epidermal inclusion cyst, absent in the trichilemmal cyst.

Lipoma is a benign tumor of mature adipocytes and the most common soft tissue tumor in adults. It presents as a soft, doughy, mobile, painless subcutaneous mass, usually on the trunk, shoulders, neck, or proximal limbs, with a thin fibrous capsule that lets it slide under the examining finger. Histology shows lobules of mature fat cells indistinguishable from normal adipose tissue apart from the capsule, and many lipomas carry rearrangements of chromosome 12q involving HMGA2. Because the proliferating cells are mature and nonatypical, lipomas do not transform; features that argue instead for liposarcoma are large size, deep or retroperitoneal location, firmness, fixation, rapid growth, and pain.

sections.title: Vascular lesions: tumors that proliferate and malformations that persist

blocks.text: Vascular lesions split into two categories with different natural histories. A vascular tumor grows by endothelial proliferation, so it has a growth phase that outpaces the child and may regress. A vascular malformation is an error of vessel development that is present at birth, is lined by quiescent endothelium, and enlarges only in proportion to body growth, so it never involutes. Deciding which category a lesion belongs to answers most questions about its course.

Infantile hemangioma is the prototypical tumor. It is usually absent or only faintly visible at birth, appears in the first weeks of life, proliferates rapidly over roughly the first 6 to 12 months, then involutes slowly, with about half of lesions largely involuted by age 5 and most by age 9. It is more common in preterm and low birth weight infants and in girls. The endothelium is GLUT1 positive, which distinguishes it from other vascular lesions, and it is histologically a dense proliferation of plump capillaries that gradually fibroses and fattens as it involutes. Because involution is the rule, the consequences that matter are local and depend on site: ulceration of the surface, periocular lesions that block the visual axis and cause deprivation amblyopia, and subglottic lesions that narrow the airway.

Cherry hemangioma (cherry angioma) is an acquired benign capillary proliferation of adult life: small, bright red, dome-shaped papules a few millimeters across on the trunk and proximal limbs that increase in number with age and do not regress. Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma) is reactive rather than neoplastic. After minor trauma or during pregnancy, a lobular mass of capillaries grows over days to weeks into a friable, exophytic red nodule that bleeds profusely with slight contact and often has a collarette of scale at its base. Pregnancy-associated gingival lesions, called granuloma gravidarum, typically regress after delivery, which fits a hormone-driven reactive process. The name is a double misnomer: the lesion is neither pyogenic nor granulomatous.

Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) is a capillary malformation: a flat pink to red patch present at birth that persists, deepens in color, and may thicken with age. A lesion in the V1 trigeminal distribution raises the question of Sturge-Weber syndrome, in which a somatic activating GNAQ mutation affects one embryonic vascular field, so the same abnormal capillary development appears in facial skin, leptomeninges, and eye. The leptomeningeal angioma produces seizures, contralateral hemiparesis, and cognitive impairment, and abnormal ocular vasculature raises intraocular pressure and causes glaucoma. Nevus simplex (salmon patch or stork bite) on the glabella and nape is a separate, common finding that usually fades.

blocks.caption: Tumors have a growth phase and may involute; malformations are present at birth and stay. Onset and course identify the category before histology does.

blocks.predict: A 3-week-old infant has a 1 cm bright red raised forearm lesion that was absent at discharge and has doubled in size. Another infant has a flat pink patch over the cheek and upper eyelid present from birth. Which lesion will be gone by school age, and which child needs brain and eye evaluation?
blocks.explain: The raised, late-appearing, growing lesion is an infantile hemangioma, a tumor that involutes. The flat patch present at birth in a V1 distribution is a capillary malformation that persists and carries the Sturge-Weber association, so leptomeningeal and ocular assessment belongs to that child.

sections.title: White oral lesions: leukoplakia, oral hairy leukoplakia, and thrush

blocks.text: A white mucosal patch is white for one of two reasons: a thickened, keratinized epithelium scatters light, or a layer of organisms and debris sits on the mucosal surface. The bedside scrape separates the two, since material that wipes away was never part of the epithelium.

Leukoplakia is defined by exclusion: a white plaque that cannot be scraped off and has no other specific diagnosis. Tobacco in all forms and alcohol are the main drivers, with betel quid in some populations, and together they act more than additively. Carcinogen exposure thickens and hyperkeratinizes the epithelium and, in a proportion of lesions, produces dysplasia, so leukoplakia is the oral counterpart of actinic keratosis: a mutated field that can progress through dysplasia and carcinoma in situ to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Transformation is low in absolute terms, but risk rises with nonhomogeneous or speckled lesions, high-risk sites (floor of the mouth, lateral and ventral tongue, soft palate), larger size, and dysplasia on histology. Erythroplakia, a velvety red patch, is less common but carries higher rates of dysplasia and carcinoma because the atrophic epithelium reveals the vessels beneath.

Oral hairy leukoplakia is a corrugated, shaggy white plaque on the lateral tongue borders that also fails to scrape off, but its mechanism differs. It is Epstein-Barr virus replication in the upper layers of the squamous epithelium, with ballooned cells containing viral inclusions and marked hyperkeratosis but no dysplasia. It occurs in immunosuppression, is a classic marker of advanced HIV infection with a low CD4 count, resolves as immune function improves, and is not premalignant.

Oral candidiasis (thrush) is superficial overgrowth of Candida albicans on the buccal mucosa, tongue, or palate, seen in infants, denture wearers, users of inhaled or systemic corticosteroids, after broad-spectrum antibiotics, and in diabetes or immunosuppression. The pseudomembrane is a mat of pseudohyphae, yeast, fibrin, neutrophils, and desquamated cells lying on the surface, so it scrapes off and leaves erythematous, sometimes bleeding mucosa beneath. Potassium hydroxide or periodic acid-Schiff preparations show pseudohyphae confined to the most superficial epithelial layers, and thrush without a local explanation points to an immune or endocrine defect behind it.

blocks.title: Worked example: three white tongues
blocks.text: Three adults have white oral patches. A 62-year-old smoker has a thick white plaque on the ventral tongue and floor of the mouth that a tongue blade does not move. A 34-year-old with a CD4 count of 90 cells per microliter has corrugated white streaks on both lateral tongue borders, also fixed. A 70-year-old using inhaled corticosteroids has curd-like buccal patches that wipe away and leave red mucosa. The third is superficial Candida. Carcinogen exposure at high-risk sites makes the first leukoplakia, with its dysplasia risk, while bilateral lateral tongue corrugation in immunosuppression makes the second Epstein-Barr virus driven oral hairy leukoplakia, which carries none.

integration.text: The organizing question in this chapter is which cell proliferates and whether its checkpoints still work. Seborrheic keratosis, lipoma, cherry hemangioma, and the keratin cysts are clonal or reactive proliferations of mature, nonatypical cells, often with an activating mutation or rearrangement in a growth pathway (FGFR3 or PIK3CA in seborrheic keratosis, HMGA2 rearrangement in lipoma), but with intact p53 and Rb control, so they enlarge and stop. Actinic keratosis, dysplastic nevi, and oral leukoplakia involve the same proliferative drive plus loss of checkpoint function, through TP53 mutation from UV photoproducts, loss of p16 encoded by CDKN2A, or carcinogen-induced mutation in oral epithelium, which is why atypia appears and progression becomes possible. This explains the grading language shared with every other epithelium on the exam: hyperplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, invasive carcinoma.

Each lesion also connects outward. Anatomy and embryology explain the cysts and the vascular birthmarks: a cyst keeps the keratinization program of the epithelium it came from, and a single somatic GNAQ mutation in one embryonic field gives the face, meninges, and eye findings of Sturge-Weber syndrome. Immunology explains why immunosuppression multiplies actinic keratoses, allows EBV to replicate in tongue epithelium, and permits Candida overgrowth, and why paraneoplastic pemphigus and dermatomyositis injure skin through tumor-directed immunity. Endocrinology explains the acanthosis nigricans a learner will actually see, since hyperinsulinemia acting on IGF-1 receptors is far more common than a gastric tumor acting through the EGF receptor. The limits are worth stating plainly: the Leser-Trelat association rests on case series in an age group where both lesions are common, progression rates for individual actinic keratoses and leukoplakias vary widely between studies, and the diagnosis of a dysplastic nevus has meaningful interobserver variability.

summary: UVB forms pyrimidine dimers that become C to T mutations, often in TP53; the surviving basal clone matures poorly, which gives lower epidermal atypia, parakeratosis, and the rough scale of actinic keratosis over a dermis showing solar elastosis.

Partial-thickness epidermal atypia is actinic keratosis, full-thickness atypia with an intact basement membrane is squamous cell carcinoma in situ, and a breached basement membrane is invasive carcinoma.

A common nevus stops growing because its own BRAF or NRAS mutation triggers p16-dependent senescence; germline CDKN2A loss removes that brake, so many dysplastic nevi mark whole-body melanoma risk rather than acting as the usual precursor lesion.

Seborrheic keratosis is a bland basaloid epidermal proliferation with horn cysts and FGFR3 or PIK3CA activating mutations; it is benign at any color, but sudden eruption of many lesions is the Leser-Trelat sign.

Paraneoplastic skin signs work either through tumor growth factors (Leser-Trelat sign, malignant acanthosis nigricans, classically gastric adenocarcinoma) or tumor-directed immunity (dermatomyositis with ovarian, lung, and GI cancers; paraneoplastic pemphigus with lymphoid neoplasms); most acanthosis nigricans is simply insulin resistance.

An epidermal inclusion cyst has a granular layer and flaky laminated keratin, a trichilemmal cyst of the scalp has no granular layer and dense compact keratin, and rupture of either provokes a foreign body giant cell reaction that mimics an abscess.
Lipoma is an encapsulated mass of mature adipocytes, the most common adult soft tissue tumor, and does not transform; size, depth, firmness, fixation, and pain argue for liposarcoma instead.

Vascular tumors proliferate and may involute (infantile hemangioma appears in the first weeks, grows, then regresses; pyogenic granuloma grows in days and bleeds), while vascular malformations such as port-wine stain are present at birth and persist, with V1 involvement raising Sturge-Weber syndrome.

A white oral plaque that scrapes off is Candida sitting on the mucosa; one that does not is epithelial, with leukoplakia from tobacco and alcohol carrying dysplasia risk and oral hairy leukoplakia from EBV on the lateral tongue in immunosuppression carrying none.

verify: Annual progression risk of a single actinic keratosis to squamous cell carcinoma is quoted from about 0.025 percent to over 1 percent per lesion per year across studies; this chapter states it as a small fraction of one percent.

Malignant transformation rates for oral leukoplakia vary widely by series (commonly quoted at about 1 to 5 percent per year, higher for nonhomogeneous and dysplastic lesions); confirm whether NABNE expects a figure at all.
The proportion of seborrheic keratoses carrying FGFR3 versus PIK3CA mutations differs between studies; both are described as common activating mutations here rather than given percentages.
The strength of the Leser-Trelat association with internal malignancy is debated, since both eruptive keratoses and cancer are common in older adults; stated here as a prompt to evaluate, not proof.
Timelines for infantile hemangioma involution (about 50 percent by age 5 and most by age 9 in common teaching) vary between sources; given here as approximate.

The fraction of acanthosis nigricans that is paraneoplastic, and the magnitude of malignancy risk in adult dermatomyositis, are reported over broad ranges; confirm the figures NABNE uses if numeric answers are tested.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Leser-Trelat, Bowen disease, Gottron papules, Sturge-Weber, familial atypical multiple mole melanoma, and Gardner syndrome, or only descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: epidermal-dysplasia-grades (normal epidermis, actinic keratosis, carcinoma in situ, invasive carcinoma side by side) and cyst-wall-comparison (epidermal inclusion cyst with granular layer beside trichilemmal cyst without one).

Port-wine stain and Sturge-Weber risk are taught here by the V1 trigeminal distribution, while recent work maps the lesions to embryonic facial placode territories rather than to trigeminal dermatomes; confirm which description NABNE uses.
